cheema_2018.name: Pseudo-homogeneous Haber–Bosch process
cheema_2018.description: The paper models the steady-state operating envelope of a three-bed autothermic Haber–Bosch synthesis reactor and recycle loop for producing ammonia from hydrogen and nitrogen, with argon as an inert. It predicts bed temperatures and reactant conversions, along with operating limits, hydrogen intake, ammonia production, and recycle load as process conditions change. The pseudo-homogeneous model combines catalyst-bed material and energy balances, a modified Temkin reaction-rate law, quench mixers, and a feed–effluent heat exchanger. The authors simulate a nominal 120 kg h⁻¹ ammonia-production design in MATLAB and examine six variables relevant to flexible operation with intermittent renewable power. The model is designed using specified production and temperature targets and trial-and-error adjustment of bed volumes and flows; the paper does not report fitting or validation against new experimental data. The authors use the simulations to identify operating flexibilities and limits for power-to-ammonia plants, and provide supporting equations and simulation data in the electronic supplementary information.

facts.text: The modeled process is a Haber–Bosch ammonia synthesis reactor system and recycle loop intended for power-to-ammonia operation.
facts.quote: The focus of this work is to determine the steady-state operational and production limitations of the ammonia synthesis reactor system and recycle loop, as renewable energy will be only intermittently available for the production of the reactants.

facts.text: The modeled synthesis feed contains hydrogen and nitrogen, with argon as the inert species in the power-to-ammonia loop.
facts.quote: In the power-to-ammonia synthesis loop, the only inert gas is argon

facts.text: The reactor system uses three catalyst beds with quench-based inter-stage cooling and heat exchange between the reactor outlet and inlet streams.
facts.quote: using the quench based inter-stage cooling three bed ammonia synthesis reactor system

facts.text: The three catalyst beds have volumes of 0.0075, 0.0221, and 0.0464 m³, for a total catalyst-bed volume of 0.0760 m³.
The nominal modeled reactor pressure is 200 bar and the reactor-system intake temperature is 523 K.
Normal fresh feed is supplied at a hydrogen-to-nitrogen molar ratio of 3:1, with nitrogen feed containing 2 mol% argon and hydrogen supplied pure from storage.
facts.quote: fresh stream ① N₂ supply with 2 mol% of Ar and pure H₂ supply from storage is considered in ratio of 3 mol of H₂ to 1 mol of N₂.

facts.text: The normal reactor intake stream contains 5 mol% inert gas, and the modeled purge removes 0.0241 of the recycle-stream mass fraction.
facts.quote: A concentration of 5 mol% of inert gas is maintained in the reactor system intake stream ③ by purging 0.0241weight fraction of recycle stream ⑤.

facts.text: The nominal design targets 673 K at the inlet and 773 K at the outlet of each catalyst bed, with the outlet target alternatively limited to 90% of equilibrium temperature.
facts.quote: For achieving the optimal reactor design volume with the maximum possible reaction rate, inlet temperatures of all catalyst beds are maintained at 673 K and their outlet temperature at 773 K or 90% of the equilibrium temperature.

facts.text: The nominal design produces 120 kg h⁻¹ of ammonia, excluding 1.11 kg h⁻¹ lost in the purge gas.
The model is a steady-state physicochemical, pseudo-homogeneous model comprising heat-exchanger, catalyst-bed, and mixer subsystems.
facts.quote: Physicochemical modelling is applied to analyse the ammonia synthesis reactor system under steady-state operation.

facts.text: The model calculates conversion for both hydrogen and nitrogen in each of the three beds, as well as the reacting-mixture temperature, corresponding to nine bedwise state profiles.
Catalyst-bed conversion and temperature are calculated using steady-state material and energy balances along bed volume.
facts.quote: The steady state material and energy balance for the fine catalyst particles in catalyst beds are shown

facts.text: The ammonia formation rate uses a modified Temkin equation developed by Dyson and Simon, with activities used instead of partial pressures.
The catalyst-bed model represents the exothermic synthesis of ammonia from hydrogen and nitrogen and accounts for equilibrium effects.
facts.quote: The reaction takes place at the surface of the catalyst, where nitrogen and hydrogen are consumed, and ammonia is formed in an exothermic reaction.

facts.text: The catalyst is assumed to be magnetite Fe₃O₄, and the paper discusses fine catalyst particles of 1.5–3 mm.
facts.quote: For fine catalyst particles of size 1.5 to 3 mm

facts.text: The feed–effluent heat exchanger is represented with an ε-NTU effectiveness model, and its effectiveness is held constant during the stability analysis.
facts.quote: The ε-NTU model has the advantage over conventional methods as it does not require evaluation of mean temperature differences and detailed design of the heat exchanger.

facts.text: The heat-exchanger effectiveness used for normal operation is 0.6329.
facts.quote: The effectiveness of heat exchanger ε = 0.6329, which is calculated by using eqn (2) for normal operation temperature range.

facts.text: The differential equations are implemented in MATLAB using the built-in ode45 solver.
facts.quote: The simulation is performed in MATLAB software and a built-in ODE solver (ode45) is used for the implementation of differential equations.

facts.text: Bed volumes, feed flow, and quench flow rates were adjusted by trial and error to meet the nominal ammonia-production target.
The model stops the design reaction at 90% of equilibrium composition because reaching equilibrium would require infinite reactor space.
facts.quote: For design only, the reaction is considered to be accomplished when reaching 90% of the equilibrium composition, as for equilibrium conversion operation an infinite amount of reactor space is required.

facts.text: The paper reports simulation-based analysis rather than parameter fitting or validation against new experimental measurements.
The paper states that limitations from the separation section, including the coolers and ammonia separator, are excluded from the analysis.
The operating-envelope analysis varies reactor pressure, inert concentration, ammonia concentration, hydrogen-to-nitrogen ratio, total flow rate, and reactor-system inlet temperature one at a time.
facts.quote: During the steady-state stability analysis one process variable is changed and the other five process variables are held constant.

facts.text: The authors use van Heerden plots to identify steady states and their stability; the upper stable branch is preferred because it gives maximum conversion.
facts.quote: The upper steady state point is desired for operation due to stability and maximum conversion.

facts.text: The stable operating pressure range is 194.32–213.91 bar, with the upper limit set by the catalyst-bed temperature limit.
facts.quote: The stable operational envelope for pressure is 194.32 to 213.91 bar.

facts.text: The modeled inert concentration range is 0–12.73 mol%; concentrations above 12.73 mol% prevent autothermic operation.
The desired operating range for ammonia concentration in the reactor feed is 3.39–4.53 mol%.
The modeled hydrogen-to-nitrogen operating range is 1.18:2.82 to 3.05:0.95, and operation at the low ratio reduces hydrogen intake by about 67% while raising recycle load.
facts.quote: The reactor can be operated for H₂-to-N₂ ratios between 1.18 : 2.82 and 3.05 : 0.95.

facts.text: The low hydrogen-to-nitrogen boundary reduces modeled ammonia production by about 73% and increases the recycle-to-feed ratio by about 257%.
Total feed flow can be varied from 527.78 to 707.61 kg h⁻¹; the low-flow case produces 100.60 kg h⁻¹ ammonia and the high-flow case 116.13 kg h⁻¹.
facts.quote: The maximum and minimum total feed flow rates are 707.61 to 527.78 kg h−1 respectively, with corresponding ammonia productions of 116.13 and 100.60 kg h−1.

facts.text: The reactor-system inlet-temperature range is 519.41–536.84 K, with the upper limit associated with the maximum catalyst temperature.
facts.quote: The operating envelope for the feed temperature is between 519.41 and 536.84 K

facts.text: The paper identifies inert concentration and hydrogen-to-nitrogen ratio as the largest flexibility levers, with hydrogen intake reductions of up to about 67%.
The model indicates that reducing the hydrogen-to-nitrogen ratio can decrease reactor temperature by up to 90 K.
facts.quote: the reactor temperature decreases by up to 90 K with decrease in H₂-to-N₂ ratio

facts.text: Operation beyond the modeled envelope can end autothermic operation or overheat and damage the catalyst.
facts.quote: Operating outside these boundaries leads to the shutdown of reactor system autothermic operation or damage to the catalyst due to overheating.

facts.text: The authors note that unmodeled heat losses could affect the operating envelope in smaller plants or at very low feed rates.
facts.quote: For smaller scale plants and very low mass feed flow rate, these losses might be noticeable and influence operating envelope.

facts.text: The model follows the three-bed pseudo-homogeneous dynamic reactor model of Morud and Skogestad (1998), while this paper analyzes steady-state operation and uses a static heat-exchanger representation.
facts.quote: Morud and Skogestad in 1998 analysed the Haber-Bosch process with a pseudo-homogeneous dynamic model for a three catalyst bed reactor system and a static model for a counter current heat exchanger

facts.text: Mancusi et al. (2000, 2001, 2009) used heterogeneous reactor models and reported qualitative agreement with pseudo-homogeneous results, with shutdown pressure and feed-temperature differences reported in the cited studies.
facts.quote: Mancusi et al. in 2000, 2001 and 2009 analysed the same process with a heterogeneous model and concluded substantial qualitative agreement with the pseudo-homogeneous results

facts.text: Azarhoosh et al. (2014) compared a one-dimensional heterogeneous model with plant results and reported catalyst-bed temperature differences up to 13.5 K; Farivar and Ebrahim (2014) later reported a 4 K difference using a two-dimensional model.

Unlike the equilibrium-based Haber–Bosch loop analysis of Cinti et al. (2017), the paper uses a kinetic reactor model; it also distinguishes itself from Sánchez and Martín (2018) by considering an autothermic synthesis reactor.
facts.quote: For the Haber-Bosch loop, thermodynamic equilibrium is considered instead of a kinetic approach, which is suitable for design-based analysis only.

facts.text: The authors present the model as a way to assess whether an autothermic Haber–Bosch reactor can continue operating flexibly during renewable hydrogen shortages.
The electronic supplementary information provides additional model equations and supporting simulation data.
facts.quote: Additional equations for heat exchanger, catalyst beds and ammonia synthesis loop, along with supporting simulation data are provided.
